hints: Think about what a voltmeter actually measures when it is connected between two different half cells in one circuit.
Recall the three standard condition values that must be fixed for concentrations, temperature and gas pressure to make the measurement comparable.
walkthrough:
Picture what is being compared**
You have two separate half cells joined together. Each one has its own tendency to gain or lose electrons. When you connect them, electrons flow and you read a voltage. That reading is the cell potential, the difference between the two half cell potentials.

Add the word standard**
Standard means you fix everything that could change the value. Keep temperature at 298 K, keep any gas at 1 atm pressure, and keep every ion concentration at 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Only then is the measured potential difference a standard cell potential, $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$.

Final answer: The potential difference between two half cells / electrodes.
Measured under standard conditions of 298 K, 1 atm for gases and all solutions at 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.

hints: Remember that any standard electrode potential is always measured against the same reference half cell, the standard hydrogen electrode.
List what each side needs: a Pb rod in $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ solution on one side, and a Pt electrode in $\text{H}^{+}$ solution with $\text{H}_{2}$ gas on the other.
Think how the two solutions are joined electrically without mixing, and how the potential difference is read.
Check that every chemical is labelled with its standard state: 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ solutions, 1 atm $\text{H}_{2}$, 298 K.
walkthrough:
Set up the Pb half cell**
Place a clean Pb rod into a beaker containing $\text{Pb}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$ at 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. This is a metal/metal ion electrode, so the metal itself conducts electrons out to the circuit.

Set up the standard hydrogen electrode**
In a second beaker place 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)}$, for example HCl. Dip in a Pt electrode, which is inert and just carries electrons. Bubble $\text{H}_{2}$ gas at 1 atm over the Pt surface using an inlet tube, so the equilibrium $2\text{H}^{+}+2\text{e}^{-} \leftrightharpoons \text{H}_{2}$ is established on Pt.

Complete the circuit**
Join the two solutions with a salt bridge containing a saturated inert electrolyte such as $\text{KNO}_{3}\text{(aq)}$. This allows ions to move and maintains charge balance without mixing the solutions.

Measure the potential**
Connect the Pb and Pt electrodes with wires to a high resistance voltmeter. Label the voltmeter V, label all chemicals and electrodes, and state standard conditions of 298 K. The reading is $E^{\ominus}$ for $\text{Pb}^{2+}/\text{Pb}$ because the hydrogen electrode is defined as 0.00 V.

Final answer: Left beaker: Pb(s) electrode in 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Pb}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$. Right beaker: Pt electrode in 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)}$ with $\text{H}_{2}$ gas at 1 atm bubbled over Pt via delivery tube. The two beakers joined by a salt bridge. Electrodes connected via external wires to a voltmeter.

hints: Write the reduction equilibrium for the lead electrode: $\text{Pb}^{2+}+2\text{e}^{-} \leftrightharpoons \text{Pb(s)}$ and think which side is favoured if $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ is removed.
Link less tendency to reduce to a more negative electrode potential, since reduction becomes less favourable.
walkthrough:
Apply Le Chatelier to the half cell**
For the reduction direction $$\text{Pb}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^{-} \leftrightharpoons \text{Pb(s)}$$ decreasing $[\text{Pb}^{2+}]$ removes reactant. The system opposes the change by shifting left to make more $\text{Pb}^{2+}$, favouring the oxidation direction.

Translate to voltage**
A shift left means the electrode is less easily reduced, it gives up electrons more readily. Its tendency to act as a positive cathode falls, so the measured E moves to a more negative value compared with the standard value of -0.13 V.

Final answer: Tick: more negative.
Lowering [$\text{Pb}^{2+}$] shifts the equilibrium $\text{Pb}^{2+}+2\text{e}^{-} \leftrightharpoons \text{Pb(s)}$ to the left, favouring oxidation, so E becomes more negative than $E^{\ominus}$.

hints: Start from $Q = It$ and remember to convert the 80 minutes into seconds to get charge in coulombs.
Use the given half equation to find the mole ratio: 2 moles of electrons convert 1 mole of Pb, then multiply moles of Pb by $A_{r}$ of Pb.
walkthrough:
Calculate total charge passed**
Charge is current times time in seconds: $$Q = It$$ $$Q = 0.40 \times 80 \times 60 = 1920 \text{ C}$$ This is the total electrical charge delivered by the cell.

Convert charge to moles of Pb**
Each Pb atom releases 2 electrons: $$\text{Pb(s)} + \text{SO}_{4}^{2-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{PbSO}_{4}\text{(s)} + 2\text{e}^{-}$$ Moles of electrons $= Q/F = 1920/96500$. Moles of Pb is half of that: $$n(\text{Pb}) = \frac{1920}{2 \times 96500} = \frac{1920}{193000} = 9.95 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$ Then mass $= n \times A_{r}$: $$m = 9.95 \times 10^{-3} \times 207.2 = 2.1 \text{ g}$$
Final answer: $Q = 0.40 \times 80 \times 60 = 1920$ C. Moles Pb $= Q / 2F = 1920 / 193000 = 9.95 \times 10^{-3}$ mol. Mass Pb $= 9.95 \times 10^{-3} \times 207.2 = 2.1$ g.

hints: Balance the extra two O atoms in $\text{PbO}_{2}$ by adding water to the right, then balance H and charge with $\text{H}^{+}$ and electrons on the left.
walkthrough:
Balance the reduction at $\text{PbO}_{2}$**
Pb goes from +4 in $\text{PbO}_{2}$ to +2 in $\text{PbSO}_{4}$, so 2 electrons are gained. The two oxide O atoms need 4 $\text{H}^{+}$ to form 2 $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Adding $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ gives the precipitate: $$\text{PbO}_{2}\text{(s)} + \text{SO}_{4}^{2-}\text{(aq)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{PbSO}_{4}\text{(s)} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O(l)}$$ Check atoms and charge: both sides have 1 Pb, 6 O, 4 H, 1 S and zero net charge.

hints: Compare a closed box containing a fixed amount of $\text{Pb}$, $\text{PbO}_{2}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ with a cell fed from external tanks.

Think what happens to reactant concentration and voltage as $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ is consumed to make $\text{PbSO}_{4}$ and water, versus when $\text{H}_{2}$ and $\text{O}_{2}$ are constantly replenished.
walkthrough:
Why the lead-acid voltage drops**
A lead-acid cell is a closed system. As it discharges, solid $\text{Pb}$ and $\text{PbO}_{2}$ are both converted to $\text{PbSO}_{4}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ is consumed to give water. Once the active materials run low and acid concentration falls, the cell chemistry can no longer maintain the same potential, so the voltage curve drops sharply.

Why the fuel cell stays flat**
An $\text{H}_{2}/\text{O}_{2}$ fuel cell is an open system. Hydrogen and oxygen are fed in continuously from outside and product water is removed. Reactant concentrations at the electrodes never deplete, so the electrode potentials and therefore the overall voltage stay constant over time.

Final answer: Lead-acid cell: reagents $\text{PbO}_{2}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ are used up / their concentration decreases, so voltage falls after several hours.
Fuel cell: fuel $\text{H}_{2}$ / $\text{O}_{2}$ is continuously supplied so concentration stays constant and voltage remains constant.
